t: How To Use Mystery To Captivate Your Students https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2013/05/25/how-to-use-mystery-to-captivate-your-students/
q: One of the best ways to do this is with small doses of mystery. When sprinkled here and there like the first wisps of snowfall, it has a unique way of cutting through the distractions of modern childhood.
Storytelling is inherently mysterious. Because it invites students to follow along with you down a winding path to who knows where.
Allowing students to think for themselves improves independence, sparks animated conversation, and fills the room with a sense of surprise.
It is the mystery of why, after all, that draws students in and gives them reason to care about what you’re teaching.
Although it takes some forethought, leaving strategic gaps of information out of your lessons and stories can fuel great interest.
The truth is, over-explanation takes the fun and intrigue out of learning.

t: Why Difficult Students Need Your Unconditional Acceptance nal-acceptance/
q: Effective classroom management requires you to hold difficult students accountable beyond just the four walls of your classroom.
Everyone on campus knows who they are and are quick to point out their transgressions.
Thinking too much, too often, and too critically about one's performance can cause unrelenting stress and anxiety. It causes athletes to freeze up, salespeople to fumble their presentations.
Simply following your classroom management plan is enough for her to understand that she made a mistake.
She needs to know that her mistakes don’t define her and that even if she were to mess up every single day, you would still be in her corner and on her side.
Your most difficult students need not your red-faced lectures or your bitter disappointment, but your forgiveness, your grace, and your unconditional acceptance.

t: A Non-Freaked Out, Focused Approach to the Common Core — Part 5 — Every Kid Speaks
q: Prior to the Common Core, I nurtured a belief that not all of my students needed to talk. After all, some are shy (I was, too, as a secondary school student), and mandatory speaking events can bring about fits of visceral terror for the introverted.

They all seemed to suggest that simply getting every student reading, writing, and talking would do much to prepare students for a diverse array of post-secondary demands. And so it came to be that I grew convinced enough to implement three simple strategies for ensuring every student spoke just about every day.

Whenever it's time to call on students to share their thinking on an issue, a text, or a question I've posed, I use the index cards. If I can work through a deck each class period, I have ensured that every student has spoken at least once.
My goal isn't to create classes of public speakers, but it is to enable my students to live choice-filled lives. If they choose to pursue professions that require no public speaking, great!
I am vigilant in creating a safe space for my students. Meanness is out of place and unacceptable. My students know they won't be mocked for not having it all together.

I model the value of failure. My students know that those who deliberately practice in their areas of weakness have a huge advantage over those who don't. They know that I am the most expert failer in the room because I've failed the most and I aggressively learn from failure.
Yet, as I look at my students and how they've grown in confidence and skill, I'm thankful I dared to expect every one of them to participate in each of our speaking/listening events.
x: Stuart explains how he moved from believing shy students need not talk to requiring every student to speak almost every day.
Stuart explains how he moved from believing shy students need not talk to requiring every student to speak almost every day.
A deck of student index cards, worked through each period, is his low-tech guarantee that every student speaks at least once.
He answers objections that not everyone needs public speaking, that anxiety harms introverts, and that tests won't assess it, arguing his goal is choice-filled lives rather than producing orators.
He reports non-cooperation under 1% and attributes it to rehearsal time, a safe classroom where meanness is unacceptable, modeling failure, grading and quietly logging non-participation.
Near-universal participation comes from rehearsal time, a safe no-mockery culture, modeling failure, light grading and not making a scene over refusals.
The piece closes by urging nervous teachers to expect participation from every student.

t: How To Handle A Student Who Habitually Calls Out https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2013/05/11/how-to-handle-a-student-who-habitually-calls-out/
q: Namely, how do you deal with a student who, despite receiving consequence after consequence, continues to call out in class?
Like a lion cub that doesn’t get enough to eat, she has learned that she must assert herself or get pushed to the margins.
She also needs to know that you will never respond to her when she calls out. Hearing this plainly and clearly from you will relieve a good deal of the internal stress that is causing the habit.
Instead, make brief but pleasant eye contact with her (2-3 seconds) and then call on someone else.
When you do notice her sitting quietly with her hand raised—and you will—casually call on her like you would any other student.
Responding to students who call out is the very thing that encourages it—along with encouraging a host of other disruptive behavior.

t: Non-Freaked Out Common Core — Part 4 — Argument and Debate
q: But don't just take my word for it. In an article back in 2011, gurus Jerry Graff and Mike Schmoker (their books Clueless in Academe, They Say / I Say, and Focus have hugely shaped me) warned that, though the CCSS held promise, especially compared to the preceding generation of state-created wish lists, there was still too much fluff. Their fear was that the high impact standard of argument might get watered down amongst the rest.

This is problematic; many will not read the appendices and, as a result, will likely spread their curriculum too thin by trying to equally teach all 10 of the basic writing anchor standards. The simple problem with trying to equally teach all 10 is that, frankly, it can't be done well, at least not by an average teacher like me.

Emphasize and exploit the strong link between spoken and written argumentation. I think this is one of the keys for making argumentative writing accessible. When students can enjoy, participate, and dominate in classroom debates, they begin to see and understand the beauty of crafting great arguments in writing.

From the first day to the last, we simply do lots of arguing. I've found no activity besides reading and writing that match it for the power to enhance my students' self-concepts, academic abilities, and character strengths. Seriously.

Below, I'll walk you through the lesson for the day of the debate; for what it's worth, this was one of the best debates I've yet seen. Remember, the reason debates work well in my class is because I invest a good amount of time into them throughout the year — it's not because I'm some magical debate coach.

Teacher feedback (5 minutes): I then give students what I noticed. I use specific examples and student names, and I both praise and critique. This is a time for us to get better, not a time to give fake praise or avoid the truth.

I've found this to be an especially effective format when I grade them on two croosch moves: 1) their ability to paraphrase the speaker they are responding to, and 2) their ability to make their own point with support from evidence and/or logic. After doing this form of debate last Friday, I caught my students paraphrasing in a much less structured classroom discussion this week.

He grounds it in Graff and Schmoker's 2011 warning that argument's 'special place' in the CCSS is buried in an appendix and will be diluted if teachers try to teach all ten writing anchor standards equally.
Stuart insists the spoken-written link is the accessibility lever — students who can enjoy and win classroom debates start to see why crafted written arguments matter.
His closing case for debate is non-instrumental: it changes how students see the world, forces them to hold both sides of an issue, and transforms the task of reading and writing arguments.
His debate lesson is engineered against the usual failure modes.
The fourth installment of Stuart's non-freaked out Common Core series makes a single high-leverage recommendation: have students argue, frequently, in every subject.

The pop-up debate is his most transferable format: no teams, no moving seats, students stand when ready, and the grading targets exactly two moves — paraphrase the previous speaker, then make your own evidence-backed point.

t: How To Avoid An Increase In Misbehavior As The School Year Winds Down s-the-school-year-winds-down/
q: It’s common for behavior to worsen during the final few weeks of the school year.
Sensing summer break approaching, students begin to feel their age outpacing their grade level. They grow restless and excitable.
Knowing that a downward trending of behavior is a possibility, it’s smart to reaffirm your classroom management plan before the dip occurs.
It’s best to reteach your plan as a refresher rather than an angry response.
With testing in the review mirror, many students will conclude that the school year is essentially over, which is a surefire predictor of misbehavior.
Reach the finish line, not with the exhausted, salt-encrusted visage of a marathon runner, but with a sprinter's bounce in your step.
x: Maintain or increase academic pace and rigor through the final weeks.
Behavior commonly worsens near year's end as students sense summer approaching and test whether classroom boundaries remain firm.
Preemptively reteach the classroom management plan before any downward trend begins, rather than reacting after it starts.
